walkthroughs.body_html:
King John lost Normandy in 1204 and raised heavy taxes.

Barons rebelled and forced him to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. It said the king must obey the law, couldn't jail nobles without trial, and couldn't tax without consent. Clauses 39 and 40 became foundations of liberty.

Henry III ignored Magna Carta. Earl Simon de Montfort led barons to victory at Lewes in 1264.

In 1265 he called a parliament with two knights from each shire and two burgesses from each town — the first with elected commoners. Edward I copied this in his Model Parliament of 1295.

The Tudors strengthened monarchy after 1485.

Henry VIII used Parliament to break with Rome (1534 Act of Supremacy). Elizabeth I used progresses and propaganda. But Parliament still controlled taxation — a power that would clash with the Stuarts after 1603.

mcqs.q: What did Magna Carta actually do in 1215?
options: It was a peace treaty between King John and rebel barons protecting baronial privileges and limiting arbitrary royal taxation and imprisonment — it was annulled within months.
Magna Carta gave ordinary English people democratic rights and freedom.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
Magna Carta abolished the monarchy and created Parliament.

mcqs.q: What did the 1832 Great Reform Act actually do?
options: It abolished rotten boroughs, redistributed seats to industrial towns, and extended the vote to about 1 in 5 adult men — still far short of democracy.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
The 1832 Reform Act gave the vote to all working men.
The 1832 Reform Act allowed women to vote for the first time.
